opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing people get wrong is assuming "good data" means "correct data." Correctness is necessary, but it's almost the floor, not the ceiling.

For me, good AI data has a few properties. The first is that it actually teaches the model something it doesn't already know. A lot of data, even very clean data, is redundant. If the model can already do the task, another ten thousand examples of it just burns compute. So good data lives near the edge of the model's capability: hard enough to matter, but not so noisy or ambiguous that the signal disappears.

The second is that it reflects real expertise and real reasoning, not just the final answer. When we work with domain experts, a doctor, a lawyer, a strong mathematician, the most valuable part usually isn't the answer they give. It's how they got there: what they considered and ruled out, where they were uncertain, what tradeoffs they made. That process is what the model needs to learn, and it's also the hardest thing to capture. Most people, even experts, don't naturally write down their reasoning in a way that's useful.

The third is consistency of judgment. If you give the same type of problem to ten annotators and get ten different standards, the model learns confusion. So a lot of the work is designing the rubric and the process so that "good" means the same thing across thousands of people. That's actually much more of an operations and product problem than people expect.

And the last piece is that data quality is relative to what you're trying to build. Data that's great for pretraining might be useless for post-training. Data that improves a benchmark might not improve how the model feels to a real user. So I always ask: good for what? The best data is the data that closes a specific gap you've identified in the model. That's why I think the data side and the model side have to work very closely. You can't produce great data in isolation from understanding where the model is failing.

r001.rationale: The response discusses different domains and data uses, but does not identify diversity of scenarios as a contributor to data quality.

r002.rationale: It says valuable data comes from domain experts such as doctors, lawyers, and mathematicians, and emphasizes capturing their reasoning.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that "good" data is less about any single property and more about fit: does the data actually teach the model something it couldn't already get for free?

When people first think about this, they usually fixate on quantity. More tokens, more examples, bigger crawl. And that worked for a long time, because the models were starved. But once you've scraped most of the open web, the marginal web page is worth almost nothing. The model has already seen a thousand pages like it. So the question shifts from "how much" to "what does this example add that the previous ten million didn't."

That pushes you toward a few things. First, correctness. If you're training on reasoning, math, code, anything where there's a right answer, a wrong example isn't neutral, it actively teaches the model a bad habit. One confidently wrong solution can undo a lot of good ones, because the model learns the style of confidence without the substance. So verification matters more than volume. Can you run the code? Can you check the proof? Can you have a second person independently reach the same conclusion?

Second, diversity, and I mean real diversity, not surface variation. Ten thousand customer service dialogues that all follow the same script are basically one example repeated. What you want is coverage of the hard cases, the ambiguous ones, the ones where a smart human would pause and think. Those are rare in natural data precisely because they're hard, so you often have to go out and deliberately construct them.

Third, and this is the one people underrate, the data has to reflect the judgment you actually want. When you ask humans to label or write examples, you're not collecting facts, you're collecting taste. Which answer is better? When should the model push back? How much detail is appropriate? If your annotators are rushed, or they don't understand the domain, or the instructions are vague, the model inherits that sloppiness very faithfully. So a lot of what makes data good is invisible in the data itself. It's the quality of the people, the clarity of the rubric, the feedback loop where you look at disagreements and figure out why.

And finally, you have to look at it. That sounds trivial, but a lot of teams treat data as a pipeline, numbers go in, loss goes down, and nobody reads the examples. Every time I've seen a data problem get fixed, it started with someone actually opening a few hundred rows and going, wait, this is wrong. The metrics tell you something is off. The reading tells you what.

So if I had to compress it: good data is correct, it's hard, it's varied, it encodes the judgment you want, and somebody has actually read it.

r001.rationale: The response says good data needs real diversity and coverage of hard, ambiguous cases, including deliberately constructed examples.

r002.rationale: The response identifies the quality and domain understanding of annotators who label or write examples as affecting the data.

astra-6.text:
I think good AI data starts with a clear question: good for what? Data that helps a model write poetry may not be what you need to help it interpret a financial report.

Then I’d look at accuracy, relevance, and coverage. Does the data contain reliable information? Does it reflect the situations the model will actually encounter? And does it include difficult cases and different perspectives, rather than thousands of copies of the easy examples?

The labels matter, too. If people disagree about what a good answer looks like, adding more labeled examples can just add more confusion. You need clear standards, while preserving genuine ambiguity where it exists.

Ultimately, the test is whether the data helps the model perform better on new, realistic problems. More data is useful only if it teaches the model something worth learning.

r001.rationale: The response says data should reflect the situations the model will encounter and include difficult cases and different perspectives, identifying scenario diversity as a quality contributor.

r002.rationale: The response discusses label standards and disagreement, but does not identify the quality of people providing demonstrations as a contributor.

sol-6.1.text:
I think good AI data starts with a clear question: what do you want the model to learn? Data can be accurate and still be irrelevant to the task. So I’d look at whether it’s correct, whether it reflects the situations the model will actually encounter, and whether it covers enough variety—including the difficult, unusual cases.

And more data doesn’t automatically mean better data. Duplicates, inconsistent labels, and misleading examples can add volume without adding value. Ultimately, the test is whether the data helps the model perform more reliably on real problems, including cases it hasn’t seen before.

r001.rationale: It says good data should reflect real situations and cover enough variety, including difficult and unusual cases.

r002.rationale: It does not identify the quality of people providing demonstrations as a contributor to data quality.
